meta.method: deep-entry form: senses+context synthesized ONLY from LC/Hopkins comparanda (hgm_evidence and corpus English withheld); POS deterministic only (SOAS / tense evidence); see_also restricted to a computed candidate list of real headwords; INSUFFICIENT allowed

ka 'khor ba.gloss: cycling from the beginning; beginningless cyclic existence

senses.gloss: cycling from the beginning; beginningless cyclic existence
senses.context: Formed on ka, the first letter of the Tibetan alphabet, used to indicate a starting point; the compound conveys cycling from the very first, i.e., from the beginning. Hopkins glosses it as beginningless cyclic existence, literally 'cycling from the letter ka'.

ka cog zhang.gloss: Ka, Jok, and Zhang (the three translators)

senses.gloss: Ka, Jok, and Zhang (the three translators)
senses.context: An abbreviated collective designation for three translators: Ka-wa Pel-tsek (ka ba dpal brtsegs), Jok-ro Lü-gyel-tsen (cog ro klu'i rgyal mtshan), and Zhang Na-nam Ye-she-de (zhang sna nam ye shes sde). The term joins the first syllable of each name.
A contraction of ka nas dag pa, 'pure from ka', the first letter of the alphabet standing for the beginning. Hopkins glosses it as primordially pure, pure from the beginning, or essential purity.

ka nas dag pa.gloss: pure from the beginning; essential purity

senses.gloss: pure from the beginning; essential purity
senses.context: Literally 'pure from ka', i.e., pure from the first letter of the alphabet, hence pure from the very beginning. Hopkins renders it as essential purity or primordial purity, the fuller form of ka dag.
Tibetan phonetic transcription of the Sanskrit name Kamalaśīla.

ka tsan dbyangs gsum.gloss: the three [grammars of] Kalāpa, Candra, and Sārasvata

senses.gloss: the three [grammars of] Kalāpa, Candra, and Sārasvata
senses.context: An abbreviated enumeration of three basic Sanskrit grammatical systems, named by the first syllables of their titles/authors: Kālāpa (associated with Śarvavarman), Candra (Candragomin), and Dbyangs can (Sarasvata, associated with Anubhūti). Used as a set designation for the core Sanskrit grammarians studied in Tibet.
Tibetan transliteration of the Sanskrit kāya, "body," retained untranslated (as against the usual Tibetan rendering sku). Occurs chiefly in transliterated mantra, titles, and technical phrases.
Tibetan transliteration of the Sanskrit kālacakra, name of the tantra, its deity, and its system; translated into Tibetan as dus kyi 'khor lo, "wheel of time."
A pulse position in medical diagnosis, the pulse felt with (under) the middle finger.
Equivalent to nye ba'i nyon mongs pa, the derivative or branch afflictions attendant upon the root afflictions. Here prefaced by the enumerative syllable ka, marking it as the first item of a list.
A transliterated designation used for the inhabitants of Karṇāṭa (Karṇāṭaka). The comparanda attest only this ethnic/regional reference and give no further specification.
Transliteration of Sanskrit kārṣapaṇa, a unit of coinage. Used where texts speak of money or a monetary amount, as in reckoning a price expressed in such coins.

see_also: kar sha pa na mgron ('gron) bu stong drug brgya'i rin

senses.context: Renders Sanskrit chattra, a covering held or spread above; also glossed as canopy. In this sense it is equivalent to the simple term gdugs.
In one attested usage (marked {C}) chattra is glossed 'parachute', i.e. an umbrella-like device for descending.
Corresponds to Sanskrit samantatamas, darkness extending everywhere. The compound joins kun khyab, 'pervading all', with mun pa, 'darkness'.
A paired epithet combining omniscience (kun mkhyen) with all-seeing vision (kun gzigs). The comparanda attest only this descriptive phrase, without further specification of whom it qualifies.

An epithet rendering Sanskrit ikṣvāku, in which bu ram shing pa ("sugar-cane one") is prefixed by kun mkhyen ("omniscient"). It functions as a title of a personage of the sugar-cane (Ikṣvāku) line rather than as a common noun.
Corresponds to Sanskrit sarvārtha-siddhi (attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra): achieving, establishing, or bringing to completion the aims/welfare of all beings.

Renders ārāma-sampad / ārāmasaṃpanna, a garden or pleasure-grove that is excellent or complete in its qualities; phun sum tshogs pa conveys the sense of perfection or abundance attached to kun dga' ra ba (garden).

Given by Hopkins as "personal altar"; the spelling rwa ba is a variant of ra ba. The illustrative Tibetan passage supplied speaks of searching even behind the kun dga' rwa ba and among the rubbish, indicating a fixed household fixture or enclosure.

kun dga' rwa ba.sanskrit: tha na kun dga' rwa ba'i rgyab log dang; gad snyigs tshud chad kyi nang du zhib 'tshol byas

senses.context: Renders ānanda-śabda (attested in the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra): a sound, cry, or utterance expressing delight.

Rendered by Sanskrit ādeśanā-prātihārya, a marvel or miraculous display consisting in reading and announcing what others are thinking. The Tibetan compound joins 'brjod pa' (declaring, stating) with 'cho 'phrul' (miraculous display), the whole being characterized as 'kun' (thorough, complete).

kun nyon dang rnam byang tha dad med pa.gloss: non-difference of the thoroughly afflicted and the purified

senses.gloss: non-difference of the thoroughly afflicted and the purified
senses.context: Corresponds to Sanskrit saṃkleśa-vyavadānābheda: the absence of any difference between thoroughly afflicted phenomena (kun nas nyon mongs, saṃkleśa) and purified phenomena (rnam par byang ba, vyavadāna). Used of a topic in which these two ordinarily contrasted classes are asserted not to be distinct.
Represents the Sanskrit pair saṃkleśa-vyavadāna, the contrasting classes of thoroughly afflicted phenomena and purified phenomena.
Glossed in verbal fashion as the purifying (rnam par byang) of thorough afflictions (kun nas nyon mongs pa).
Renders the causative saṃvardhayati (from saṃ √vṛdh), a verb of causing to grow or increase; the Tibetan 'kun tu' conveys the thoroughness or completeness of the producing or engendering.
Given for saṃvega and udvega; a state of being thoroughly depressed, saddened, or disgusted. The prefix 'kun tu' marks the completeness of the sad or wearied state.
The further Sanskrit comparanda ākṣepa and saṃkopa point to a sense of being stirred up or agitated, alongside the meanings of despondency and disgust.
Renders forms of Sanskrit saṃ-√tras, of fear that is complete or all-pervading. Hopkins glosses it as 'thoroughly fear, be terrified, be frightened'.
The Sanskrit comparandum saṃtrāsayati is causative, so the expression can also correspond to causing complete terror in another.
Corresponds to Sanskrit samutpāda, glossed by Hopkins as 'production, arising, generation, engendering'. The element kun tu conveys the sense of complete or thorough production.

kun tu bskyod.gloss: thoroughly moved, shaken; caused to move

senses.gloss: thoroughly moved, shaken; caused to move
senses.context: Renders forms of Sanskrit saṃ-√kamp (saṃkampayat), i.e. complete trembling or shaking. Hopkins glosses 'thoroughly move; completely cause to go', reflecting the causative form of the Sanskrit.
Corresponds to Sanskrit saṃchādya, an absolutive; the Tibetan mdzad nas likewise marks a completed prior action. Hopkins glosses 'having completely covered'.
Corresponds to Sanskrit saṃdhāvati; Hopkins gloss 'move, wander, go', with Conze's renderings 'err about, run together'. The Tibetan ste is a connective particle linking to what follows.
Renders Sanskrit parivrājaka, a religious wanderer who has left home and roams as a mendicant. Used as a designation of such ascetics generally, including non-Buddhist ones.
In its verbal/general sense the term corresponds to āgama, āgamuka, i.e. going or moving about in all directions, with kun tu conveying 'thoroughly, everywhere'.
Feminine form of kun tu rgyu ba, designating a woman who lives as a wandering mendicant or ascetic.
Corresponds to saṃtrāsam āpadyante, 'they fall into terror'. kun tu marks the thoroughgoing or complete character of the fright.

Renders samudghātita-śukla-dharma, where dkar po'i chos are the white, i.e. virtuous, doctrines or qualities, and kun tu bcom indicates their being thoroughly vanquished or done away with. Hopkins glosses the compound rather as 'all-conquering wholesome doctrines/practices', so both a destroying and a destroyed reading are attested in the comparanda.
Corresponds to samucchinna-kuśala-mūla: the roots of virtue (dge ba'i rtsa ba) have been entirely cut off or annihilated, kun tu indicating the completeness of the severance.

kun tu 'jug.gloss: engagement in all; engaging in everything

senses.gloss: engagement in all; engaging in everything
senses.context: Rendered by Hopkins as "engagement in all," i.e. entering into or applying oneself to all (objects, activities, or aspects) without exception. The prefix kun tu conveys the sense of comprehensiveness or thoroughness attaching to the act of 'jug pa, entering/engaging.

Corresponds to Sanskrit samudghāta / samuddhāta and uccheda, terms for uprooting or cutting off completely. Hopkins gives "thoroughly destroyed, thoroughly wrecked," the kun tu marking the completeness of the destruction.
In contexts where 'joms pa has the sense of overpowering rather than annihilating, Hopkins renders the term "thoroughly conquered."

Equivalent to Sanskrit parikalpa / parikalpana (and saṃkalpa), the mental activity of constructing or imagining an object. Hopkins gives "conceptuality, thorough conceptualization, ideation, comprehensive imagination/construction."

Where the term corresponds to the past participle parikalpita, it qualifies what is produced by such conceptual activity: "imputed, imputational, imaginary, thoroughly [mentally] constructed, imagined" (Hopkins).

Corresponds to Sanskrit parikalpa-mātra, formed with tsam (mātra, "only, mere"). Hopkins renders it "imputation-only, conceptualization-only," i.e. something that is nothing more than a conceptual construction.

Hopkins gives "arisen from conceptuality, arisen from conceptualization, arisen from imputation," i.e. produced by the constructive activity of thought (kun tu rtog pa) rather than existing independently of it.
Hopkins gives this as both the act and the state of realizing something completely. Used verbally ('thoroughly realize') and nominally ('thorough realization').

Lokesh Chandra records Sanskrit saṃkalpa (from the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), i.e. a thought, conception or imaginative construction formed about an object. In this usage the phrase names the mind's thoroughgoing conceptual apprehension rather than a valid insight.

kun tu rtogs par bya ba.gloss: is to be thoroughly realized; what is to be thoroughly realized

senses.gloss: is to be thoroughly realized; what is to be thoroughly realized
senses.context: The gerundive form (bya ba) of kun tu rtogs pa, glossed by Hopkins both verbally ('is to be thoroughly realized') and as the object so realized. Lokesh Chandra correlates it with Conze's āvedhyate, a passive form.

Corresponds to Sanskrit darśana, saṃdarśana, ādarśana, nirdeśa — a complete displaying or setting forth of something to others. Hopkins renders it 'thoroughly teach / show / demonstrate / reveal / disclose'.

senses.gloss: appearing, showing up (as in a mirror); perceiving
senses.context: Conze's readings ādarśana / avadarśika are given by Hopkins as 'perceive' and 'show up [in a mirror]', i.e. the appearance or manifestation of an image rather than deliberate instruction.
With Sanskrit ākhyāna, the term denotes a narrated account or communication — what is told or made known. This nominal sense is recorded by Hopkins as 'tale; communication; advise'.

Past/perfective stem corresponding to kun tu ston pa, matching Sanskrit ādarśayati and saṃdarśana. Hopkins gives 'thoroughly teach; thoroughly show; thoroughly demonstrate; thoroughly reveal; thoroughly disclose'.

senses.gloss: shown up (in a mirror), made to appear
senses.context: Conze's ādarśayati is glossed by Hopkins as 'show up (in a mirror)', i.e. causing an image or thing to become manifest.

Lokesh Chandra records Sanskrit ākarṣaṇa (from the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra), the act of drawing or pulling toward oneself; Hopkins renders the Tibetan as 'thoroughly lead'. The sense is thus of completely drawing or guiding something (or someone) along.
